claims.text: RHEAs exhibit superior high-temperature mechanical strength relative to conventional refractory alloys with simpler compositions.
RHEAs exhibit modified thermoelastic behavior relative to conventional refractory alloys with simpler compositions.
Complex multi-element compositions generate enhanced local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions impede dislocation motion.
Local lattice distortions slow atomic diffusion.
Impeded dislocation motion and slowed diffusion produce higher high-temperature yield strength.
Enhanced lattice distortion produces altered elastic recovery and thermal-expansion behavior under high-temperature loading.
Reducing the number of principal elements minimizes lattice distortion.
Identical heat-treatment protocols ensure a consistent single-phase solid-solution microstructure in both compositionally different alloys.
The high-entropy variant will have higher yield strength than the conventional refractory-alloy baseline at 800–1200°C.
The high-entropy variant will have a slower creep rate under constant load than the baseline.
The high-entropy variant will differ from the baseline in elastic modulus during high-temperature testing.
The high-entropy variant will differ from the baseline in elastic recovery during thermal cycling.
The proposed mechanism applies under inert-atmosphere service at approximately 800–1200°C.
The predicted behavior may not persist at lower temperatures.
Secondary-phase formation may invalidate the predicted behavior.
The magnitude of the predicted improvements depends on exact compositional balance and microstructural uniformity.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and predictions require an altered or different thermoelastic response, which need not be an improvement, whereas the falsification rule requires a statistically significant improvement in thermoelastic response. Thus, a significant alteration that is not classed as an improvement could satisfy the prediction but trigger the stated falsification rule.
